webTitle: What AOC gets right – and wrong – about ‘Woke 1.0’ | Francine Prose

fields.headline: What AOC gets right – and wrong – about ‘Woke 1.0’
fields.trailText: Recent comments by AOC have reignited a fiery debate about ‘wokeism’. But what are we really talking about?
fields.bodyText: Full confession: I am one of those who have come to think that Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez can essentially do no wrong. At times when I most fear for the future of our country, I watch her videos and am consoled and cheered by her clarity, her honesty, her intelligence, her simple common sense. So I was a little surprised to hear that on a recent interview on ABC This Week, she quoted a political ally as having remarked: “Woke 1.0 was crazy.” What surprised me was not that she called for some moderation of the radical positions – the call to defund the police and the military, for example – that have, at times, been an aspect of progressive politics. But I was frankly a little unnerved to hear her use the word “woke”. The term has its roots in Black slang. “Stay woke” was originally a warning to keep alert to the dangers posed by prejudice and white supremacy. But its meaning has changed to become a synonym for what used to be referred to, also derogatorily, as “PC” – politically correct. I’ve politely asked my colleagues at the college where I teach to avoid the word because it has so effectively been weaponized by the far right to mock and discredit anyone who supports racial justice, economic equity, universal healthcare, and many of the issues in which I too believe. In the ABC interview, AOC explained the ways in which, during the Covid lockdown, “There was a huge opening. The doors were really open to entertain any and every policy that was trying to get us to a better place. But the rhetoric we used at that time is not the rhetoric we use today.” She went on to explain that her primary goal – improving the life of every American – has remain unchanged. Even though I wish she’d used different language for it, I understand her suggestion that Woke 1.0 was crazy. The strict policing of language, the “cancellation” of anyone who had, at any point in their life, made a mistake that was perceived as injurious to women or people of color, the inflexible and frequently impractical notions of what can be said, taught and legislated raised the specter of a dictatorial left that devalued individual liberties and threatened our freedom of speech almost (though not quite) as much as the extreme right. In the current issue of the Atlantic, there’s an eloquent and terrifying essay by Tyler Austin Harper, explaining why the absurd and damaging policies regarding the need to root our racism in the college curriculum and in the larger society made him decide that he – a Black scholar with a tenure-track appointment to teach interdisciplinary humanities in an environmental-studies program – had no choice but to abandon academia forever. In 2021, it was decided that every department at Bates College, where Harper worked, must offer two courses that would “identify areas where white supremacy, ‘colonial’ frameworks, and other forms of bias might be lurking in curricula and major requirements”. This would include the science classes, taught by faculty who often had no idea how to address these complex topics. Such courses might include a math class aimed to help students understand “the role of mathematics as a gatekeeper and driver of injustice”. A colleague suggested that when a student or teacher made a remark perceived to be insensitive, another student should call out “oops” or “ouch” as a helpful corrective. Though some of the more extreme policies were eventually rescinded, the final effect was to make Harper decide that he no longer felt capable of functioning with any degree of personal freedom and integrity on a college campus. The policies implemented at Bates were, I assume, typical of the Woke 1.0 ideology to which AOC was referring. Policies like those, which were heavy-handed interventions in curricula and teaching norms – and the headlines they generated – made it all too easy for the far right to ridicule the ideals of the more moderate and left-leaning Americans, and to use that ridicule as a tool to make sure that the old-fashioned, constitutionally guaranteed aspects of our democracy – including freedom of speech and assembly – could be characterized as “radical” and even “communist”. The infighting and mutual recrimination that this inspired between progressive and centrist Democrats made it all too easy for the right to dismiss the worthiest of ideals – freely available healthcare, childcare and education, an end to inflation and to the profiteering that has enabled billionaires to widen the income disparity so harmful to average US families – as the kind of folly that allowed the Bates community to describe an argument between white and Black students as a “lynching”. So once again, I agree with AOC. We need to focus on what’s politically viable, on what is attainable, on what the American people so desperately need. Censorship and repression are not only counterproductive but destructive, regardless of whether those efforts come from the right or the left. The midterms are approaching. Our country stands on the brink of a brighter or a much, much darker future. Let’s concentrate on coming together to represent the real needs and interests of our citizens and not on the labels – “woke” or “ultra-conservative” – that only deepen the problems of a nation in which the average family must so often choose between feeding the children or paying the rent. Francine Prose is a former president of the PEN American Center and a member of the American Academy of Arts and Letters and the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. Her latest book is Five Weeks in the Country

webTitle: Trump dismisses concerns about USS Abraham Lincoln, saying its record-breaking 250 days at sea ‘not nearly enough’ – as it happened

fields.headline: Trump dismisses concerns about USS Abraham Lincoln, saying its record-breaking 250 days at sea ‘not nearly enough’ – as it happened
fields.trailText: This live blog is now closed.
fields.bodyText: The Trump administration has asked ⁠the ⁠US supreme court to allow construction of his controversial $400m ⁠White House ballroom to proceed after an ‌appeals ‌court ordered work to halt. In a case testing Donald Trump’s presidential authority, the Washington-based US ⁠court of appeals for the District of Columbia circuit ruled last week that the controversial ‌project lacked the necessary approval from US Congress. It’s worth noting that the appeals court ruling blocks the above-ground construction of the ballroom, but would allow the work on the underground security structure to continue. However, the government argues that “every part” of the project is “an integrated whole geared toward remedying security deficiencies and bringing critical improvements to the White House”. The administration add in its filing to the court: “The entire ballroom structure is designed to shield the military installation beneath it.” Also today, Trump dismissed the reports about the mental health crisis and living conditions on board USS Abraham Lincoln. When he was asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation, the president said “no, they’re not.”The vessel has now been on a record-breaking deployment for more than 250 days, but Trump said that it had not been at sea for too long. “Not nearly enough,” he said. The president also confirmed that the USS Abraham Lincoln would now be replaced by another aircraft carrier. Trump threatened to declare strait of Hormuz a ‘territory of the United States’. During a speech at the a police academy on Long Island, New York, he repeated his frequent claims that Iran “is being very badly defeated” as peace talks with Iran remained at an impasse fand Tehran refused to reopen the strait – one of the world’s busiest oil shipping channels – which has been all but closed since the US and Israel launched a war on Iran in February. Trump also insisted that his administration is “bringing the prices way down” despite the fact that the latest data shows that overall inflation is up 3.4%, compared to a year ago. A woman was arrested on Friday morning in connection with the vandalization of the second world war memorial on the National Mall in Washington DC, the capital’s federal prosecutor announced. Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, announced mid-morning that a suspect was in custody and the justice department is filing two felony charges against her. The memorial had graffiti scrawled on it and the pool polluted with soapy bubbles. The woman accused appears to have live streamed the incident on Facebook. More here A federal court in Nevada dismissed the Department of Justice’s case seeking to compel states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls. The court was the 22nd consecutive court to reject the Trump administration’s campaign to obtain private data in its efforts to find evidence of voter fraud. The Republican Texas senate candidate Ken Paxton has been entangled in an array of scandals – fraud and bribery allegations, infidelity claims and a hyper-local ordeal where he was accused of stealing a $1,000 pen. James Talarico, Paxton’s Democratic opponent in the race, has notched an endorsement from the local attorney Joe Joplin to whom the pen belonged. Talarico’s campaign put out an ad titled “Ken Paxton steals pens” with security footage from 2012 showing Paxton picking up the opulent Mont Blanc pen at a Dallas area courthouse. At the time, Paxton’s camp rebuffed claims of theft, maintaining it was a mistake. The pen was later returned to Joplin. During a speech at a police academy on Long Island on Friday, Donald Trump stressed several times that his White House is staffed by young, “gorgeous, beautiful girls”, who constantly thank him for seizing control of policing in Washington DC. “Every day I come to the White House, people are thanking me. ‘Thank you, sir.’ ‘Thank you.’ ‘Thank you sir’”, Trump began, before fixating on the youth and beauty of the female staffers he said were praising him. “These young, beautiful girls, these young, beautiful girls, these young, beautiful girls in the White House, you know, they come in. Now, I’m not supposed to say ‘beautiful’, but what the hell!” the president continued. “These young, these gorgeous, beautiful girls, they want to be safe,” he went on. And they come- ‘Mr President, may I speak to?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Thank you, sir, thank you.’ I said, ‘Why are you thanking me?’ ‘Because a year and a half ago, I was afraid to leave- I was afraid to open the door of my apartment. And now I walk to the White House every morning and I have absolutely no fear. Thank you, sir.’” Bulldozers have begun plowing up ground at the mouth of Big Bend national park’s famed Santa Elena Canyon as part of the Trump administration’s multibillion-dollar “smart wall” expansion on the US-Mexico border, according to new footage taken by activists who have been monitoring the site. Tensions have run high since the Trump administration announced plans to erect new border security infrastructure in the roughly 500-mile Big Bend region of south-west Texas, which includes the Lone Star State’s largest and most-visited national park. Since last week, activists have shared video footage that appeared to show heavy machinery laying the groundwork for new border infrastructure that US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) did not announce and initially denied was happening. By Thursday, photographer Natalie Newman captured video footage of bulldozers plowing earth at the mouth of the Santa Elena Canyon, a frequently visited stretch of the Rio Grande flanked by 1,500ft cliffs. “It’s just devastating,” said Laiken Jordahl, a public lands advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. “They’re bulldozing a brand new road through the most beloved stretch of the park.” Democratic lawmakers have continued to criticize the Trump administration’s response to reports of distress on the USS Abraham Lincoln Adam Schiff, the California senator wrote on X: “Listen to what Trump said about servicemembers suffering a lengthy deployment onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln… He said they have not been deployed ‘nearly long enough.’ Easy to say when you spend your time golfing at Mar-a-Lago.” Ruben Gallego of Arizona wrote: “Cadet Bone Spurs thinks he understands what happens on deployments,” making referene to the president’s 1968 medical draft exemption for bone spurs in his heels, which excused him from service during the Vietnam War. On his way to New York earlier on Friday, Donald Trump approached reporters with a copy of a news headline he wanted them to see. Holding up a print-out of the headline, “Prescription drug prices record sharpest drop in more than 60 years”, the president waved the print-out around and encouraged the press pool to record and photograph it. “The headline today is exactly that,” he said proudly. “Did you see it?” He then read the good news aloud and held up the print-out again, which displayed the headline and the first five lines of the article, for the cameras. “Okay, got it? Everybody have it?” he asked. What the president did not explain is that the text of the article, published by the Washington Post on Thursday, reported that while the Trump White House “took credit for” the biggest year-over-year drop in drug prices in more than 60 years in July, independent experts “said a Biden-era policy that requires Medicare to negotiate prices for some popular prescription drugs is more likely to be driving down costs.” “The Inflation Reduction Act was a signature accomplishment of former president Joe Biden, a sprawling measure enacted in 2022 that aimed to lower prescription drug prices by requiring Medicare, the federal health program for the elderly, to begin negotiating the prices it pays drugmakers for an array of popular and costly prescription drugs,” the Post’s report noted. “The first price reductions took effect at the beginning of this year.” The Post also quoted Richard Frank, a professor emeritus of health economics at Harvard University, expressing doubt Trump’s policies were behind the drop in drug prices. “If I was a betting guy on what mattered most, it would be probably stuff around the Inflation Reduction Act,” Frank said, adding that Trump’s efforts “wouldn’t be where I’d place my money.” A federal court in Nevada dismissed the Department of Justice’s case seeking to compel states to turn over their unredacted voter rolls. The court was the 22nd consecutive court to reject the Trump administration’s campaign to obtain private data in its efforts to find evidence of voter fraud. The administration has not found any substantial evidence of fraud, and critics and election experts have said the effort to obtain voter information is another attempt to sow distrust in the system. The DOJ has sued sued 30 states and Washington DC to try to force secretaries of state to hand over the data. On Friday, US district judge Anne Traum said she was “joining every other court to have addressed the issue so far” in her ruling. Here’s more background on the administration’s effort, and why even red states are pushing back: The acting secretary of the navy, Hung Cao, again denied poor conditions and a mental health crisis on board USS Abraham Lincoln. “The USS Abraham Lincoln crushed their deployment and will return home soon as part of a planned rotation,” Cao said in a post on X. “Unfortunately, the media are trying to paint our warriors as victims.” Here’s more from my colleague Edward Pilkington, who reported on the crisis aboard the aircraft carrier: Two leading specialist military papers, the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes, are reporting that there have been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard as poor conditions and mental stresses on the Lincoln reach the breaking point. The crew is in its ninth month at sea, and has spent 250 days consecutively without making land – a record for an aircraft carrier in modern times. Worried families vented their anxieties about loved ones onboard the Lincoln at an emotional town hall meeting with navy leaders in San Diego last Thursday, Stars and Stripes reported. One spouse among the 200 or so family members said that her husband had texted her that day saying “he hopes he doesn’t wake up tomorrow”. The families’ worries were expressed directly to navy leadership, represented at the town hall by the acting navy secretary, Hung Cao, and other top officials. A woman at the meeting told Cao that the navy had “broken trust between us and the leadership”, the paper reported. The Navy Times gave details of thwarted suicide attempts onboard the aircraft carrier during the current deployment. Annabelle Loma told the outlet that her husband had tried to jump overboard after his spell at sea kept being extended. “He’s scared. He thinks he’ll get a dishonorable discharge, and just because he was burnt out his 13-year career is ruined, just like that,” she said. The paper quoted another sailor’s wife whose husband was involved in a separate incident onboard the Lincoln in which he prevented a fellow crew member from jumping, grabbing them and bringing them back on deck. Trump has wrapped up his speech to to law enforcement on Long Island. He wrapped up with his usual refrains against DEI. As he left the stage, he told Fox News on Iran: “We’re capable of destroying the whole place. If they hit, we would hit back 100 times harder.” Trump insisted that his administration is “bringing the prices way down” despite the fact that the latest data says that overall inflation is up 3.4%, compared to a year ago. He repeated his frequent claims that Iran “is being very badly defeated”, despite the fact that a peace deal remains elusive. “Pretty soon I’ll be declaring the Hormuz strait a territory of the United States.” The president also brushed off the hike in US gas prices while addressing law enforcement officers in Long Island: “So remember that when you have to pay a little bit more, you’re at $4, it’s OK … I mean, I’ll never apologize. I did the right thing.” The president also touted his executive order that directs the justice department to the pursue the death penalty for anyone convicted of killing a law enforcement officer. However, it’s worth noting that Donald Trump issued pardons for more than 1,500 people involved in the January 6 insurrection, including those who assaulted Capitol police officers. When he returned to the White House last year, Trump also directed the justice department to dismiss all pending indictments against people related to the Capitol riots. At his remarks in Long Island, Donald Trump said that Washington DC is now “one of the safest cities” in the country, claiming that “crime is down 81%”. However, total crime in the nation’s capital is actually only down by 20% at the point in 2026, compared to last year, according to data compiled by the DC police department. Digging in further – assault with a dangerous weapon increased by 40% compared to this time last year in Washington DC. And overall violent crime is actually up 4% compared to this point in 2025. Trump has often taken credit for the crime reduction in DC, after a spike in 2023. But violent crime actually dropped by 29% between 2024 and 2025 – at the end of the Biden administration. A reminder that Trump addressed law enforcement in Long Island back in 2017, in a now infamous speech. At the time he talking about his crackdown on foreign gang members to an audience of police officers and the relatives of victims of crime in Brentwood. The president spoke dismissively of arresting officers who protect suspects’ heads while putting them in police cars. “And when you see these thugs being thrown into the back of a paddy wagon,” he said, “you just see ’em thrown in, rough.” Trump added: “I said, ‘Please don’t be too nice.’ Like when you guys put somebody in the car and you’re protecting the head. You know? The way you put the hand over [the head], like ‘don’t hit their head’ and they’ve just killed somebody.” “I said, ‘You can take the hand away,’ OK?” Press secretary Karoline Levitt briefed reporters aboard Air Force One en route to New York, saying they expect thousands at today’s event and a heavy law‑enforcement presence. She noted that attorney general Todd Blanche and FBI director Kash Patel will attend. Levitt declined to get ahead of treasury secretary Scott Bessent, but said the administration has “more tools” to “continue punishing Iran and crippling their economy.” She also said keeping gas prices low and preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon are “equally important” to the president – a shift from Trump’s recent focus on ending Tehran’s nuclear ambitions even if prices at the pump rise temporarily. “We want to keep gas prices low,” Levitt said. “But also ensuring Iran can never get a nuclear weapon is the president’s priority with respect to the ongoing conflict.” The national average for a gallon of gas is now just over $4, per AAA – nearly a dollar higher than this time last year. People detained at an overcrowded federal immigration camp in Mississippi were sickened by a mystery gas leak, then denied medical care when they complained of headaches and other symptoms, it has been alleged. A lengthy power outage at Adams county detention center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) facility run by the private operator CoreCivic, also left it without air conditioning for two days this week, according to one detainee who contacted the Guardian through his family. As a result, he said, people detained there were forced to spend hours outside in near 100F heat in blazing sunshine and with no shade, or left to swelter inside in cramped cells. Tensions at the center, he said, were rising, and more arguments and physical altercations were taking place between people there, leaving him and others fearful of violence that he said inadequate staffing levels would not be able to handle. The allegations come as a third person who was held in ICE custody at the Delaney Hall detention center in New Jersey, run by the GEO Group, another government contractor, was reported to have died; and an inspection report of the Adams county facility in Natchez found 23 violations of use-of-force or restraint standards. More here Trump is now en route to New York, where he’ll deliver remarks on public safety in Long Island at 3pm ET. The reporters traveling with the president today note that his outgoing press secretary Karoline Leavitt is on board Air Force One today. Trump has yet to announce Leavitt’s replacement. As he left Washington, Donald Trump dismissed the reports about the mental health crisis and living conditions on board USS Abraham Lincoln. When he was asked by reporters whether family members were worried about the situation, the president said “no, they’re not.” The vessel has now been on a record-breaking deployment for more than 250 days, but Trump said that it had not been at sea for too long. “Not nearly enough,” he said. The president also confirmed that the USS Abraham Lincoln would now be replaced by another aircraft carrier. On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the USS George Washington would be sent to relieve the Abraham Lincoln, after it was redirected to help with the military operation in Iran. “That ship is moving right now or very shortly and it’s being replaced with another very similar ship,” Trump said. A progressive group has endorsed a 27-year-old substitute teacher who overcame childhood homelessness in his bid to unseat the veteran Democrat Debbie Wasserman Schultz in Florida. The Progressive Change Campaign Committee (PCCC) said it was backing Elijah Manley in next week’s primary election in Florida’s newly drawn 20th congressional district, casting the race as a contest between a young economic populist and a stalwart of the Democratic party establishment. Wasserman Schultz, 59, an 11-term congresswoman and former chair of the Democratic National Committee (DNC), has faced criticism from African American leaders over her decision to run as the sole white candidate in a majority-minority district where she is not a resident. This followed the creation of gerrymandered congressional maps by Florida Republicans that broke Wasserman Schultz’s current seat into five shards. She decided against running in the 22nd district, where she lives, and chose instead to compete in the deep blue 20th, which has been represented by Black Democrats for more than 30 years. Yvette Clarke, chair of the Congressional Black caucus, told the Politico website on Friday: “It’s a painful situation. To have a beloved colleague who made a decision basically to run in a district where historically there’s been CBC representation, and I know that the community has been really disrupted by it.” Other candidates in the primary include former congresswoman Sheila Cherfilus-McCormick, who resigned in April over allegations of misusing $5m in federal funds, which she denies; former Broward County mayor Dale Holness; and community activist Luther “Uncle Luke” Campbell, a rapper best known for his role in 2 Live Crew. Hands Off the Arts, an artist and worker advocacy coalition, have released a statement in response to the Kennedy Center’s vote to once again to move forward with Donald Trump’s controversial plan to temporarily shutter the building for substantial renovations, which includes inscribing Trump’s name on the facade. “The Kennedy Center belongs to the American people – not one man,” the statement reads. “This vote is fatally flawed for a simple reason: To our knowledge, the board vote proceeded without figures showing how much money the institution currently has or any analysis of how a closure of this scale would affect its operation. The Center consistently has refused to release the full financial picture of profit and loss to the board or the public.” “This paves the way for more corruption,” it continues. “The President is using the Kennedy Center as another lure for people to influence him openly. The more projects that he can ‘create’ that need private donations—Freedom250, the Ballroom, FIFA events—the more avenues he has to accept gifts from people who have government interests.” The Kennedy Center board – mostly handpicked, staunch allies of the president – voted “to close the Kennedy Center’s main building” for renovations despite a federal order for Trump’s name to be removed from the signage. In May, the US district judge Christopher Cooper ordered Trump’s name to be removed from the building’s facade after the president had it added last year. Cooper ruled that the addition had been illegal, as only Congress had the authority to change the institution’s name. The center removed Trump’s name in June, but is appealing the decision. Donald Trump has confirmed that Kevin Rideout, an American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October, has been released back to the US. “I am proud to announce that Kevin Rideout, a wonderful Christian Missionary, is back in United States Custody,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform on Friday. “Kevin, the United States of America looks forward to welcoming you HOME. Glad to have helped!” Rideout, a 50-year-old missionary pilot, was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Serving in Mission International, Rideout’s organization, said earlier that he “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family. Rideout had been working in Niger for 19 years as a missionary before the incident. Read more: The woman accused of vandalizing the World War II memorial in Washington DC appears to have live streamed the incident on Facebook. A Facebook account under the name of the suspect, Melissa L Farris, currently hosts an over 30-minute video apparently live streamed on Thursday. The video shows a woman with a can of spray paint who proceeds to spray the memorial. “It was me, I’m doing it, I did it, it’s on camera,” the woman can be heard saying in the video around the 9-minute mark. This week, Donald Trump admitted that he took a military jet to leave Turkey after the Nato summit in July, despite leading the press and public to believe he was on Air Force One. Reports also emerged that the deception included smuggling the president, and some of his closest aides, on to a catering truck to avoid suspicion. In this week’s episode of Politics Weekly America, Jonathan Freedland talks with Tara Setmayer of the Seneca Project about why the White House felt the need to come up with such an elaborate lie to protect Trump. It’s worth noting that Miller’s Pac has donated to several Republicans in competitive House races this midterm cycle. Politico was first to report on the filings. These representatives include Tom Barrett, who is fighting to hold on to Michigan’s seventh congressional district. Meanwhile, Bryan Fitzpatrick, Ryan Mackenzie and Rob Bresnehan all received thousands from the Dependable Conservative Leadership Pac as they defend their central Pennsylvania House seats. The latter two congressman flipped their districts red in 2024. Mike Lawler, the Republican congressman who represents a purple district in upstate New York, said that he does not plan to return the $10,000 his campaign received from the Max Miller’s Dependable Conservative Leadership Pac. Miller is facing several domestic abuse allegations from his ex-wife, and has faced calls from both parties to end his re-election bid and resign from Congress. In an interview on Thursday on CNN, Lawler defended his decision to keep the funds, when pushed by anchor Dana Bash. “I know Max very well. I’ve talked to him personally over the last two years about this very difficult family situation. It’s tragic. I don’t think anybody disagrees about that. But this is something that should play out in family court,” Lawler said. “Max has been accused. Max has also made accusations against his ex-wife. It is tragic, and obviously I don’t condone any level of abuse. But ultimately, there has been nothing that has been corroborated here.” According to Lawler’s most recent campaign finance reports he has more than $4.8m cash on hand. When asked why he wouldn’t return the Pac funding, given that it makes up a fraction of his available funds, Lawler said “the allegations have not been verified”. He added: “If there’s evidence that Max did something, then obviously there should be a thorough investigation of that, but thus far there’s been nothing to verify any of the claims that have been leveled.” Donald Trump also decried the vandalism on the World War II memorial in Washington DC. “THERE CAN BE NO GREATER INSULT TO THOSE AMERICAN HEROES ,” Trump wrote in an all-caps missive on Truth Social. However, the president repeated his claim that another monument, the reflecting pool, was subject to vandalism. This, despite the justice department dropping the charges against David Hearn, the former Olympian accused of ripping part of the pool’s lining off. Jeanine Pirro’s office said in a court filing that the actual cause of the damage was a “botched” renovation as opposed to vandalism. Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, announced mid-morning that a suspect was in custody and had been charged with federal crimes. The memorial had graffiti scrawled on it and the pool polluted with soapy bubbles. Pirro added that the justice department is filing two felony charges against the suspect, who is now in custody. “Offenses that carry penalties of up to ten years in prison,” Pirro posted on X, showing two images of a middle-aged woman, one of her with what appears to be a can of spray-paint at the scene. “Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom. Those Americans include my father and grandfather,” Pirro added in the post. US Park Police had been investigating who graffitied the words “Clean hands dirty $” in red paint on the memorial on Washington DC’s National Mall for the second world war and vandalized the fountain with soapy bubbles. The US interior department said: “The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act” and the non-profit Friends of the National World War II Memorial said the site should not be used for political expression. The government has appealed a number of lower court decisions to the supreme court this week, in the wake of temporary injunctions over the president’s attempts to curb mail-in voting. The USS George Washington is en route to the Middle East to relieve the USS Abraham Lincoln, according to reports.
